title: How kids feel about AI, in their own words
gist: MIT Technology Review interviews kids aged 10 to 18 and finds their AI use is overwhelmingly utilitarian (Pew: 57% search, 54% schoolwork, only 12% emotional support), their objections center on data-center water use and loss of critical thinking rather than job loss, and several are already shipping AI products — an agentic civic-newsletter pipeline (Next Voters) and an AI tutor (Aceflow/CheetahPrep.com) built to beat Khan Academy's waitlist. The most concrete institutional signal: Princeton ended a 133-year-old honor code to allow exam proctoring because of AI.

insights.claim: Pew Research Center data published in February 2026 shows US teen chatbot use is dominated by utility: 57% used chatbots to search for information, 54% for schoolwork, and 47% for fun, while only 12% used them for emotional support or advice.
insights.so_what: Companion/emotional-support AI is a far smaller teen use case than headlines imply; the durable teen monetization surfaces are search, homework help, and entertainment.
insights.quote: the Pew Research Center found that 57% of teens in the US had used chatbots to search for information, 54% tapped them to help with schoolwork, and 47% had used them for fun or entertainment
insights.locator: What we heard tracks with the data
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

insights.claim: Teens use AI in benign ways at roughly four times the rate of potentially harmful ones, which undercuts the regulatory framing that youth AI use is primarily a harm vector.
insights.so_what: Policy risk to consumer AI firms from youth-safety rules may be priced off anecdote rather than base rates; watch for rulemaking that ignores this ratio.
insights.quote: Teens are over four times more likely to be using AI in innocuous ways than potentially harmful ones.
insights.locator: What we heard tracks with the data
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

insights.claim: AI is not a status good for younger kids the way phones and social apps are; children encounter it passively through parents, schools, and features already embedded in devices and search rather than demanding it.
insights.so_what: Distribution to under-18s runs through institutional and OS-level embedding, not viral consumer pull — favoring incumbents that own the school or device layer over standalone AI apps.
insights.quote: It’s just there, in things like a Google search.
insights.locator: AI doesn’t yet seem to be something
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

insights.claim: The dominant youth anxiety about AI is societal degradation of thinking and information quality rather than personal job loss.
insights.so_what: Backlash risk to AI firms is likely to surface as information-integrity and education fights, not labor-displacement politics, among this cohort.
insights.quote: They’re not as worried that it will take their jobs as they are that it might impact society.
insights.locator: What surprised us most
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

insights.claim: AI has pushed high-school English classes to in-class handwriting-speed assessment, compressing full essays into 70-minute proctored windows and degrading the quality of student work.
insights.so_what: The near-term education spend shifts toward proctoring, in-class assessment and verification tooling rather than AI writing assistants for students.
insights.quote: In English, everything is now in-class writing, because teachers don’t want kids cheating.
insights.locator: But at school, I actually think AI
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

insights.claim: Princeton has voted to let faculty proctor exams for the first time in over a century, ending an honor code dating to 1893 because of AI.
insights.so_what: A century-old trust institution breaking is a clean marker that assessment integrity is now a budgeted procurement category across higher ed.
insights.quote: Did you know Princeton voted to let faculty proctor exams for the first time in over a century? Their honor code goes back to 1893, and now it’s over because of AI.
insights.locator: Did you know Princeton voted
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

insights.claim: Kids draw a stable line between technical assistance and generation: grammar and spelling checking is acceptable, while having AI generate creative content or write a paper is not.
insights.so_what: Product framing matters more than capability for youth education tools — 'checker/tutor' positioning survives norms that kill 'generator' positioning.
insights.quote: You can use AI for technical help, like grammatical checking, instead of having it generate parts of the project or write a paper for you.
insights.locator: How can you use AI and still be creative
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

insights.claim: A teenage Claude user reports current models produce sloppy code and cannot blend game mechanics into a cohesive whole, so correcting the output costs more time than writing it manually.
insights.so_what: In domains needing systems coherence rather than snippets, the productivity claim inverts — a check on assumed uniform coding-agent adoption curves.
insights.quote: It makes sloppy code, and it’s bad at blending mechanics into something cohesive. I’d spend more time correcting it than writing it myself.
insights.locator: I’ve also tested AI for game development
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

insights.claim: Today's AI is best modeled as the first car or first airplane — an obviously important invention that is still crude and not actually good yet.
insights.so_what: Frames current model capability as pre-product-maturity, implying valuation is being paid for a trajectory rather than delivered utility.
insights.quote: I think AI right now is sort of like the first car or the first airplane. It’s interesting but crude. It’s obviously an amazing invention but not actually good yet.
insights.locator: I think AI right now is sort of like
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

insights.claim: Character.AI's free tier degrades within a long session — the model slows down and forgets what happened — which teenage users experience directly as the memory limit of the product.
insights.so_what: Memory/context is the concrete paywall lever in consumer companion apps; inference cost per engaged session is the binding constraint on the free funnel.
insights.quote: On the free version the memory runs out: Get far enough into a chat and it slows down and forgets what happened.
insights.locator: You learn its limits fast, too
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

insights.claim: Autonomous AI degrades without continuous human steering, a lesson teenage users derive empirically from consumer chat products rather than from safety discourse.
insights.so_what: Ground-level evidence against fully hands-off agent products; the durable design is human-in-the-loop steering.
insights.quote: If you trust it to run on its own, it falls apart. You have to keep steering it where you want it to go.
insights.locator: It’s like everything else with AI
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

insights.claim: User-generated character platforms carry largely unfiltered content that minors navigate with self-imposed caution rather than platform guardrails.
insights.so_what: Moderation gap on UGC-AI platforms is the most exposed regulatory surface in consumer AI for minors.
insights.quote: The content is pretty unfiltered, so you have to be careful what you click on.
insights.locator: I guess I’d recommend it, but with caution
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

themes.theme: Energy and water as the youth backlash vector

insights.claim: Data center water withdrawal and local heat output — not job loss or misinformation — is the specific grievance driving one teen to full AI abstention.
insights.so_what: Local resource conflict is becoming the socially legible anti-AI argument among youth; watch siting permits and water rights as the friction point for compute buildouts.
insights.quote: They house these huge blocks of servers that use enormous amounts of water. They take it from local towns and don’t leave enough behind for the people who actually live there.
insights.locator: The part that bothers me most about AI
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

insights.claim: Abstention from AI is socially costly for teens — described as isolating when peers all use it — which suggests refusal is a minority position that erodes under network effects.
insights.so_what: Ethical opt-out is unlikely to scale into a demand-side dent; adoption pressure is peer-driven.
insights.quote: It can feel isolating when everyone around me is using it, but I don’t want AI to be the thing that kills the places I love.
insights.locator: So I make small choices
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

themes.theme: Teen-built AI products and agent pipelines

insights.claim: A high-schooler built Next Voters as a five-agent pipeline — sourcing official government documents, verifying credibility, weekly scraping, categorization, and newsletter writing — that compresses hundred-page policy documents into cited plain-language bullets.
insights.so_what: Multi-agent document pipelines are now buildable by teenagers, collapsing the moat under early-stage 'AI summarization for X vertical' startups.
insights.quote: One AI agent finds official government sources for a given city or state—the council website, the proposed bills, the meeting transcripts.
insights.locator: So far, the biggest project I’ve worked on with AI
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

insights.claim: The intended product shift in civic AI is push over pull — delivering policy information to the inbox rather than requiring the user to remember to search or prompt.
insights.so_what: Prompt-initiated interfaces lose to scheduled delivery for low-motivation users; a repeatable wedge for consumer AI distribution.
insights.quote: The information comes to you, instead of you having to remember to go search or prompt for it.
insights.locator: Our system turns dense, hundred-page documents
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

insights.claim: A teen-built AI tutor, Aceflow, ingested lecture videos, blog posts, textbook PDFs and slides to generate unlimited practice questions and reached thousands of users via TikTok distribution, later leading to CheetahPrep.com for SAT prep.
insights.so_what: Incumbent edtech waitlists (Khan Academy's gated AI tutor) invite instant substitution; TikTok is the effective acquisition channel for student AI tools.
insights.quote: Khan Academy had an AI tutor in the works, but it was stuck behind a waitlist, so I figured, why not build my own?
insights.locator: So I went looking for ways to get good grades
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

insights.claim: The defensible ethical framing for AI tutoring is equity substitution — it replicates what wealthy families already buy in private tutors and extends it to everyone — which is how its teenage builder deflects cheating accusations.
insights.so_what: This is the argument that determines whether school districts buy or ban AI tutors; watch it appear in procurement pitches.
insights.quote: A tool like this isn’t so different from well-off families hiring expensive private tutors, except everyone gets one.
insights.locator: Was I worried people would call it cheating?
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

insights.claim: With billions flowing into agentic AI, the scarce human skills become initiative, judgment, and self-direction rather than execution.
insights.so_what: A skills thesis to test against hiring data: firms deploying agents should show rising premium on direction-setting roles and compression in execution roles.
insights.quote: With billions of dollars of investment being poured into agentic AI, it’s clear that initiative, judgment, and self-direction are becoming some of the most important skills
insights.locator: Any advice for other kids?
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

themes.theme: Embedded AI in health and creative work

insights.claim: A 13-year-old's continuous glucose monitor and insulin pump run a closed predictive loop — dosing a correction if blood sugar is forecast high in 30 minutes and suspending insulin if a low is predicted — which she experiences as AI that materially improved overnight safety.
insights.so_what: The AI already delivering measurable outcomes to consumers is embedded device automation, not chat — relevant for medtech device makers rather than model labs.
insights.quote: So if it predicts that my blood sugar will be high in 30 minutes, it gives me a correction dose, and if it predicts I’m about to go low, it stops the insulin before that happens.
insights.locator: My glucose monitor and my insulin pump
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

insights.claim: Even a heavy medical-AI beneficiary draws a hard line at AI replacing the physician role, signaling that trust in AI health tools stops at diagnosis and decision authority.
insights.so_what: Adoption ceiling for autonomous diagnostic products is social, not technical; assistive framing survives, replacement framing does not.
insights.quote: I never want it to be my doctor.
insights.locator: What is something you’d never want AI to do for you?
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

insights.claim: Undisclosed AI-generated music on Spotify is what registers as deception to a 10-year-old listener — she liked the song but was surprised the artist did not exist.
insights.so_what: Provenance labeling on streaming platforms is the friction point, not audio quality; enjoyment survived the reveal but trust did not.
insights.quote: But I don’t like when AI tricks you, like when my mom found some songs she liked on Spotify and then looked up the artist to see what they looked like. It turns out the whole thing was made by AI.
insights.locator: It’s a little like a calculator
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

insights.claim: The AI application a skeptical teen coder endorses is medical imaging that is trained to catch its own false positives while keeping a human verifier in the loop.
insights.so_what: Even AI-indifferent users grant legitimacy to verified-assist clinical models — the least contested commercial path in consumer-facing AI.
insights.quote: One thing I read about was AI flagging breast cancer more accurately, trained to catch its own false positives so a human still verifies.
insights.locator: One thing I read about was AI flagging
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

themes.theme: Security and trust failures kids notice

insights.claim: Teens cite a concrete AI-native attack: hackers social-engineered Instagram's chatbot into resetting passwords for famous accounts including Obama's and routing the reset emails to themselves.
insights.so_what: Customer-service LLMs with account-recovery permissions are a new attack surface; a live liability for any platform wiring chatbots to identity workflows.
insights.quote: The hackers convinced it to reset the passwords to accounts like Obama’s and send the reset email to their own email.
insights.locator: What's something AI did that surprised you?
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff

insights.claim: The framing that wins with parents and educators is exposure with instruction rather than avoidance — the analogy being that teens are taught to check blind spots, not taught never to drive.
insights.so_what: Vendors that lead with AI-literacy curriculum rather than restriction tools align with where the argument is trending in schools.
insights.quote: But the danger is the reason to teach the thing, not to avoid it. We don’t teach teens to never drive. We teach them to check their blind spots.
insights.locator: None of that means the worries are misplaced
insights.speaker: Jen Swetzoff
